USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold the current posture and let the May 19 trade framework execute rather than escalating or conceding. Keep the tariff threat (up to $150B, first $50B) in reserve as leverage while China works through its purchase commitments, and press the structural IP/forced-technology-transfer issues in the follow-up Beijing talks without reigniting the trade war or undercutting the ZTE penalty without adequate concession.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to US interests has fallen sharply from the April peak. The May 19 joint statement delivered a major US win — China agreed to 'significantly increase' purchases of US goods and services, and both sides put the threatened tariffs 'on hold' (Mnuchin: 'we're putting the trade war on hold'; Politico/CNN/LA Times, 2018-05-20). The US retains all leverage: Lighthizer explicitly warned tariffs, investment restrictions and export controls remain available if China fails to deliver, and Kudlow said tariffs 'have to be part of any enforcement.' Macro shows the dispute has not yet bitten the US economy — industrial production ~102.4 and rising, consumer sentiment ~98, the broad dollar index firm near 111.7, 10Y near 3.0%, WTI ~$71 (country_health). That combination — leverage plus an economy that is still strong — reads as an opportunity (-0.4 on the US anchor: extract concessions, onshore/technology posture, political upside from being tough) rather than a threat. On action, escalation would be imprudent now: the truce is working, markets rallied, and Congress is already pushing back domestically on overreaching (bipartisan Senate rebuke over softening ZTE penalties); full concession would be premature since the statement is intentionally vague with no dollar figure and structural IP issues unresolved (Schumer and CSIS's Kennedy both noted it commits neither side to specific action). The correct move is to hold, keep the tariff club visible, and hold China to execution — eschewing both escalation that could blow up the cease-fire and concession that would squander newly won leverage.
key_factors: May 19 joint statement: China pledges to 'significantly increase' US purchases; tariffs put on hold
US retains tariff leverage (up to $150B, first $50B) in reserve; Lighthizer/Kudlow keep enforcement tools available
No real-economy damage yet: IP ~102.4 rising, sentiment ~98, dollar firm ~111.7, oil ~$71
Statement deliberately vague — no dollar figure, structural IP/forced-tech-transfer issues unresolved
Congressional pushback against softening ZTE penalties signals domestic constraint on escalation
Deal framework fragile; economies warn of 'periodic ceasefires' and possible resumption of tensions

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold the current trajectory and continue negotiating within the May 19 truce framework — keep the trade war 'on hold' by honoring the agreed purchase increases and remaining open to a ZTE resolution, while not making new unilateral concessions. Press for relief on the ZTE ban as part of the ongoing talks (the U.S. administration is reportedly open to a preliminary deal that swaps some ZTE mitigation for board changes and fines), but avoid escalating tariffs or non-tariff retaliation, which would put the $150B tariff threat and the ZTE ban back into force against our export economy.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is elevated but not existential. The dispute has moved from open escalation to a fragile truce: the May 19 joint statement put the trade war 'on hold' with China committing to 'significantly increase' US purchases (Washington Times/PBS), and Mnuchin confirmed planned tariffs on up to $150B of Chinese goods are off the table while talks proceed (NYT). The fundamental threat drivers remain real — the April 3 Section 301 list targets ~$50B of Chinese aerospace, ICT, robotics and machinery (our core tech-export sectors), and the April 16 US Commerce ban has forced ZTE to halt operations, exposing our heavy reliance on US components (Qualcomm chips, Android/Google) (Guardian). The failed push to free ZTE during the talks shows our leverage is limited on firm-level issues even as the broader truce holds. This sits near the +0.5 'firm-level targeting + major export sectors hit' anchor, tempered by the fact that no tariff has yet been implemented and the truce gives room to negotiate; hence +0.4. Action leans mildly toward de-escalation (+0.1, negotiate) because escalation would be self-defeating: hitting back re-arms the very $150B tariff threat and deepens the ZTE disruption, while a controlled truce protects our export economy and preserves our own leverage (soybean retaliation targeted at US agricultural/rust-belt constituencies, per PBS/Guardian). We should keep negotiating to secure ZTE relief and avoid locking in structural IP/purchase concessions beyond what we've already committed.
key_factors: May 19 joint statement puts trade war 'on hold'; tariffs on up to $150B of Chinese goods suspended while talks proceed
April 3 Section 301 proposed list targets ~$50B of Chinese aerospace/ICT/robotics/machinery — core tech-export sectors
April 16 ZTE ban (US component cutoff) forces operational shutdown; ZTE relief unresolved after talks
China's soybean retaliation gives leverage over US agricultural/rust-belt constituencies
No tariffs yet implemented; China committed to 'significantly increase' US purchases without a numerical target
